title: Pa·s, cP, Poise: The Three Names for Dynamic Viscosity
h1: Dynamic viscosity — Pa·s, cP and poise conversions
description: 1 Pa·s = 10 P = 1000 cP. Water at 20 °C is 1 cP. Oil at 40 °C is 30–500 cP. SI insists on Pa·s; industry keeps cP.

hero: Rheology never abandoned centipoise. 1 cP = 1 mPa·s exactly — an accident of unit design that keeps everyone reading each other's datasheets.
body: Dynamic viscosity is the shear stress divided by shear rate. SI puts it in Pa·s; industry left it in centipoise. The factor is a clean 1000, and the coincidence 1 cP = 1 mPa·s is why nobody bothers switching.

> 1 Pa·s = 10 poise (P) = 1000 centipoise (cP)
> 1 cP = 1 mPa·s = 0.001 Pa·s
> 1 P = 0.1 Pa·s
Water: 1.002 cP. Blood: 3–4 cP. SAE 30 motor oil at 40 °C: ~85 cP. Honey: 2000–10 000 cP. Peanut butter: 250 000 cP. Air: 0.0181 cP.
cP: petroleum, pharmaceutical, food, paint. Pa·s and mPa·s: SI-strict physics and engineering. Poise: older physics texts, some polymer literature.

Laminar flow of 40 cP crude in a 100 mm pipe at 2 m/s: ΔP/L = 32 µV/D² = 32 × 0.04 × 2/(0.1)² = 256 Pa/m. Use Pa·s and SI throughout; convert the datasheet cP to Pa·s once at the top of the calculation.
Multiply cP by 0.001 to get Pa·s. Water is 1 cP by design.

faqs.a: No — cP is dynamic viscosity; cSt is kinematic viscosity (ν = µ/ρ). Divide cP by density in g/cm³ to get cSt.
Yes, exponentially. Motor oil at 100 °C is roughly 10× less viscous than at 40 °C. Grades like SAE 5W-30 quantify this.
